# Actors, roles, responsibility and authority

For participant wording in reusable descriptions, follow the accepted [human/agent authoring convention](../../application/problem-context-and-actor-language.md#interpreting-human-and-agent). It does not grant authority or replace the conceptual distinctions proposed here.

Candidate distinctions: an **actor** participates in activity; a **role** describes a position or set of expectations held by an actor in a context. A role is not the particular person or tool filling it.

“Owner” is too ambiguous unless the obligation and authority are named. Distinguish performing work, being answerable for the result, deciding exceptions, approving changes, and accepting an outcome. One person may hold all of these; shared responsibilities still need explicit boundaries and handoffs.

An ongoing obligation is provisionally a responsibility that persists or recurs. Completing one review or payment may discharge one occurrence without ending the continuing obligation. Whether obligation is its own primitive remains open.

For a human/agent/tool arrangement, say what each is authorized to do, what needs human judgment, and who receives a failed or ambiguous handoff. Do not infer human acceptance from an agent's success message or a workflow's completed status.

[PROV-O](../../../../source-locators.md#source-4ba3b6a5c02fa703) offers comparison terms for agents, attribution and association; we have not adopted its responsibility semantics as our complete governance model. EOM-05 remains open in [the ledger](../../../../source-locators.md#source-c43947fdcdae322a); [execution](../../execution/behavior-and-responsibility.md) develops these relationships.

<a id="participants-and-needs"></a>

## Participant descriptions and need attribution — proposal

The accepted authoring convention supplies human/agent labels. The following distinctions explain how to use richer participant declarations without treating every noun as a new primitive:

| Distinction | Meaning in a case |
| --- | --- |
| Participant kind | Human, AI agent, or the proposed programmatic participation category under this document convention. These are contextual labels with possible implementation overlap, not an exhaustive classification of entities. |
| Role | A function or position in the arrangement, such as maintaining the standard, applying it, authoring or reviewing. One participant can hold several roles. |
| Group | A specified collection of participants, such as intended human readers. State the membership boundary or what is unknown about it; membership does not imply unanimous needs. |
| Instance | A particular participant filling a role. Use distinct case labels when different humans or agents must be distinguished; do not infer distinct individuals merely from distinct roles. |
| Stakeholder | A person, group or organization whose interests can be affected by the arrangement, whether or not it directly uses the system. This is a proposed local meaning, not adoption of an external agent ontology. |
| User | A participant using the arrangement in the declared context. A user can also occupy other stakeholder or responsibility roles. |

Attach a need to the participant, role or group whose desired condition it expresses, then separately record who reported it or whether it is inferred. A claim for a role is a scoped modeling statement, not a universal psychological claim about every person who could hold that role. A group may contain competing views that require separate statements.

For a requirement, distinguish the affected participants from the subject expected to meet it and the parties implementing or assessing it. For example, the standard artifact can be the subject of a requirement intended to help human readers, authored by an agent, adopted by a human decision-maker, and supported by S1/S2. See [requirement origins](requirement.md#requirement-origins-and-contribution--proposal) and [competing needs](../../assessment/competing-needs-and-tradeoffs.md).

<a id="programmatic-participants"></a>

## Programmatic participants — proposal

The human has directed that the model represent ordinary software consumers as well as human and agent participants. The working term **program** identifies a participant performing a declared task through a specified programmatic interface. It does not mean every piece of software: an AI agent is also implemented in software. These labels describe participation in this model rather than mutually exclusive universal kinds or a ranking of intelligence, speed or scalability.

A program can be modeled as a bounded **system** when its internal parts and behavior matter. The same thing can therefore be a programmatic consumer relative to one interface and a system at another level of description. An agent may call a program, and a larger system may contain human, agent and program participants. Describe those relationships rather than inferring them from the prefix. For a hybrid participant, state which behavior and interface are being discussed.

The program's “need” in this context means an operational prerequisite for its declared function. It can be the direct consumer of an output while humans, organizations or other arrangements are affected by the result. Keep the consumer's input condition separate from the justification for selecting that consumer or function. Performance and interpretation limits belong in explicit requirements and evidence, not in an assumed human–agent–program capability ranking.

Label examples under the accepted dot convention: `human.standard.maintainer`, `human.standard.user`, `agent.standard.author`, `agent.standard.reviewer`, and `program.standard.validator`. The [authoring convention](../../application/problem-context-and-actor-language.md#category-first-references-and-programmatic-participants) explains their local meaning. The prospective validator is an illustrative consumer, not an implemented tool or an accepted machine interface.
